sites.name: Museum of Modern Art
sites.note: Irwin's first scrim installation, made for a small MoMA gallery and shown 24 Oct 1970 – 16 Feb 1971. The room is long gone; MoMA also holds his acrylic disc Untitled (1968).

sites.name: Pace Gallery
sites.work: Represents Robert Irwin and his estate
sites.note: Irwin's New York gallery. Not a permanent installation — but the place his late light works surface most often in the city.
sites.how: A 35-minute walk down Ninth Avenue, or the C/E to 23rd St.

sites.name: Dia Chelsea
sites.work: Excursus: Homage to the Square³ (1998–99), premiere
sites.note: Irwin built Excursus here in the old Dia Center for the Arts — a maze of scrim chambers lit by fluorescent tubes. Dismantled in 1999 and rebuilt at Dia Beacon sixteen years later.
sites.how: A 35-minute walk, or the C/E to 23rd St.

sites.name: Whitney Museum of American Art
sites.note: The Whitney owns it outright — a gift of the artist, accession 77.45: a 114-foot scrim bisecting a gallery, with a black line at eye level. Made for the fourth floor of the old Breuer building, not this one.
sites.how: A/C/E to 14th St, then five blocks west.

sites.name: The Breuer Building
sites.work: Scrim veil—Black rectangle—Natural light — original site
sites.note: Irwin made the scrim veil for this floor, under Breuer's trapezoidal window. It was reinstalled here in 2013, the last time the work stood in the room it was measured to.

sites.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art
sites.note: A gift of Louise and Leonard Riggio. In the collection; on view only sometimes.

sites.name: Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum
sites.note: Part of the Panza gift; some of the Guggenheim's Irwin holdings sit on permanent loan at Villa Panza in Italy. Check before you go.

sites.name: Dia Beacon
sites.work: Excursus: Homage to the Square³ (1998–99, reinstalled 2015) — and the building itself
sites.note: The one unmissable Irwin in range. He drew the master plan for the whole museum and its grounds, and Excursus returned to public view here in 2015 after fifteen years in storage. Months into the install he wrapped every fluorescent tube in colored gel.
sites.how: Metro-North Hudson Line from Grand Central to Beacon — about 80 minutes — then a 10-minute walk.

sites.name: Yale University Art Gallery
sites.work: A dot painting (1963–65) and an acrylic disc (1969)
sites.note: Two acquisitions that bracket his turn away from painting, hung in the Levin Study Gallery. Admission is free.
sites.how: Amtrak or Metro-North New Haven Line to Union Station, then a 15-minute walk.

sites.name: Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden
sites.work: Untitled (1969), acrylic on shaped acrylic, 53¼ in. diameter
sites.note: Bought through the Hirshhorn Purchase Fund in 1986. The Hirshhorn gave Irwin his big American retrospective, All the Rules Will Change, in 2016.
sites.how: Amtrak to Union Station, then Metro to L'Enfant Plaza. Free admission.

sites.name: Wellesley College
sites.work: Untitled (Filigreed Steel Line for Wellesley College), 1980
sites.note: His first permanent installation anywhere in the United States: a 120-foot steel band, never more than two feet tall, cut with leaf patterns and planted into the slope above Lake Waban. Outdoors, free, always there.
sites.how: Drive, or Amtrak to Boston and the MBTA Framingham/Worcester line to Wellesley. Walk toward Clapp Library.

sites.name: Harvard Art Museums
sites.note: A room-sized scrim under the Fogg's skylight, one of the first commissions after he closed his studio for good. Not extant.
sites.how: Drive, or Amtrak to Boston and the Red Line to Harvard.

sites.name: Buffalo AKG Art Museum
sites.note: Lit to Irwin's specification, the disc throws a ring of overlapping shadows that read as solidly present as the object. The far edge of the 300-mile circle.
sites.how: An hour's flight to Buffalo Niagara, or roughly seven hours by car or Amtrak's Empire Service.
